William I, also known as William the Conqueror, was the first Norman king of England, reigning from 1066 until his death in 1087. Previously the Duke of Normandy, he launched the Norman Conquest of England, culminating in his legendary victory at the Battle of Hastings. His reign fundamentally reshaped English society, politics, and language, introducing feudalism and Norman French to the elite.

William defeated the last Anglo-Saxon king, Harold Godwinson, at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day that same year, amid a riot when guards mistook the crowd's cheers for an assassination attempt. To consolidate his power and suppress rebellions in the north of England, he conducted the brutal campaign of destruction known as the Harrying of the North. He also commissioned the construction of the White Tower, which became the central keep of the Tower of London and remains a symbol of Norman authority.

A comprehensive record of his realm survives in the Domesday Book, which he ordered to be compiled in 1086. This survey detailed the landholdings and resources across England with remarkable precision. His great-grandson would be Henry II, who consolidated Angevin rule and made the empire William founded into one of the most powerful realms in medieval Europe.
